turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I must admit, Mr. Worthing, that I am not entirely convinced by your explanation. I do hope you can provide some more satisfactory proof of your ownership of 149 Belgrave Square.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I'm afraid I'm not certain I have any more proof to offer, Lady Bracknell. I was hoping that my engagement to Miss Gwendolen would be sufficient to establish my respectability.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I must say, Mr. Worthing, that I am beginning to suspect that you are not the gentleman you claim to be.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Mama, really, what is all this fuss about? I'm perfectly happy with Jack, and I see no reason why you should be questioning his character.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I assure you, Lady Bracknell, that my intention is to be a responsible and respectable husband, and I am willing to do whatever it takes to prove myself to you.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I must say, Mr. Worthing, that your willingness to do 'whatever it takes' to prove yourself is a most unsatisfactory answer. It suggests a lack of principle and a willingness to compromise one's values for the sake of convenience.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: I won't have you questioning my judgment, Mama. I know Jack well enough to know that he's a perfectly respectable and suitable husband.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I must say, I am shocked, shocked, that you, Gwendolen, would defend this...this...man without having the most basic of information about his background.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: I refuse to be lectured to by you, Mama, when you know nothing about Jack's past. I've told you, he's a perfectly respectable and suitable husband, and I won't be swayed by your doubts.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I understand, Lady Bracknell, that you may have doubts, but I assure you, I am a man of good character and a devoted suitor to your daughter.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I must insist that you, Mr. Worthing, provide me with proof of your identity and family background, lest I be forced to question the legitimacy of your courtship with my daughter.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: I won't be party to this absurd inquisition, Mama. You'll not undermine my relationship with Jack any further.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I refuse to be swayed by your protestations, Mr. Worthing, until I have seen irrefutable evidence of your family's standing and fortune.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I-I understand your concerns, Lady Bracknell, but I'm afraid I'm not in a position to provide the sort of documentation you're asking for, at least not immediately.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I warn you, Mr. Worthing, any further prevarication on your part will only serve to confirm my worst suspicions.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: I assure you, Lady Bracknell, that I am not trying to deceive anyone, and I am willing to do whatever it takes to prove my suitability as a husband for your daughter.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Mama, I must insist that you stop this inquisition at once. It's becoming quite clear that you're not interested in getting to know Jack for who he truly is.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I find your daughter's impertinence quite distressing, Mr. Worthing. It suggests a lack of discipline and a tendency to indulge in frivolous behavior.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: I'll have you know, Mama, that I'm perfectly capable of making my own decisions about whom I choose to marry, and I won't be lectured to by you about my 'impertinence'!

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: I refuse to be lectured to by my own daughter, Miss Gwendolen. Your behavior is most unbecoming, and I shall not tolerate this sort of insolence.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: I am engaged to Mr. Worthing, mamma.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Pardon me, you are not engaged to any one. When you do become engaged to some one, I, or your father, should his health permit him, will inform you of the fact. An engagement should come on a young girl as a surprise, pleasant or unpleasant, as the case may be. It is hardly a matter that she could be allowed to arrange for herself . . . And now I have a few questions to put to you, Mr. Worthing. While I am making these inquiries, you, Gwendolen, will wait for me below in the carriage.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Mamma!

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: In the carriage, Gwendolen!

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Yes, mamma.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: You can take a seat, Mr. Worthing.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Thank you, Lady Bracknell, I prefer standing.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: I feel bound to tell you that you are not down on my list of eligible young men, although I have the same list as the dear Duchess of Bolton has. We work together, in fact. However, I am quite ready to enter your name, should your answers be what a really affectionate mother requires. Do you smoke?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Well, yes, I must admit I smoke.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: I am glad to hear it. A man should always have an occupation of some kind. There are far too many idle men in London as it is. How old are you?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Twenty-nine.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: A very good age to be married at. I have always been of opinion that a man who desires to get married should know either everything or nothing. Which do you know?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: I know nothing, Lady Bracknell.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: I am pleased to hear it. I do not approve of anything that tampers with natural ignorance. Ignorance is like a delicate exotic fruit; touch it and the bloom is gone. The whole theory of modern education is radically unsound. Fortunately in England, at any rate, education produces no effect whatsoever. If it did, it would prove a serious danger to the upper classes, and probably lead to acts of violence in Grosvenor Square. What is your income?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Between seven and eight thousand a year.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: In land, or in investments?

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: In investments, chiefly.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: That is satisfactory. What between the duties expected of one during one’s lifetime, and the duties exacted from one after one’s death, land has ceased to be either a profit or a pleasure. It gives one position, and prevents one from keeping it up. That’s all that can be said about land.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: I have a country house with some land, of course, attached to it, about fifteen hundred acres, I believe; but I don’t depend on that for my real income. In fact, as far as I can make out, the poachers are the only people who make anything out of it.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: A country house! How many bedrooms? Well, that point can be cleared up afterwards. You have a town house, I hope? A girl with a simple, unspoiled nature, like Gwendolen, could hardly be expected to reside in the country.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Well, I own a house in Belgrave Square, but it is let by the year to Lady Bloxham. Of course, I can get it back whenever I like, at six months’ notice.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bloxham? I don’t know her.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Oh, she goes about very little. She is a lady considerably advanced in years.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Ah, nowadays that is no guarantee of respectability of character. What number in Belgrave Square?
